source.note: Bundled snapshot for deterministic offline use. The live files above are canonical; refresh this file from them — never hand-edit.

agentProtocol.name: discover
agentProtocol.how: head link rel=alternate (application/json), Dataset JSON-LD, or site llms.txt all point here

agentProtocol.name: fetch-index
agentProtocol.how: GET this file; it is generated from the page's own navigation and cannot drift — never hand-edit, refetch

agentProtocol.name: select
agentProtocol.how: choose entries by domain + summary; a component not in this index does not exist — do not invent

agentProtocol.name: read-register
agentProtocol.how: follow entry.url to the four-cell register; the when-not-to cell is binding and the anchor is a constraint, not a footnote

agentProtocol.name: resolve-bundles-and-rules
agentProtocol.how: auto-include bundles[]; hardRules[] may BLOCK the build — a block is a refusal with a citation, not a warning

agentProtocol.name: build-from-tokens
agentProtocol.how: GET cds/tokens.json and use token slices only — never raw hex; one spring curve; everything gated behind prefers-reduced-motion; 44px targets

agentProtocol.name: gate-to-human
agentProtocol.how: irreversible actions (money, sends, permissions) stop at a confirmation gate that authorises an exact payload, not a plan; log effects and blocked steps with the rule that blocked them

bundles.reason: the exit ships with the entrance — FTC click-to-cancel
user-generated content does not ship without report & block — App Store 1.2, EU DSA Art 16
post-purchase truth is part of the purchase
live video carries live captions — WCAG 1.2.4
an approval without an audit trail is theatre — EU AI Act Art 12
every grant change is logged — permissions and audit are one system

hardRules.rule: reject-all and accept-all are visual equals; non-essential defaults off
child-directed flows: neutral age screening, no personalised ads, data minimisation
LIVE styling on non-live content is a violation, not a style choice
no fee appears for the first time at the pay step
cancelling takes no more effort than subscribing, in-app, end to end
no asymmetric consent, guilt copy, fake scarcity, camouflaged ads, or retention mazes; conflicts escalate to the human
agent surfaces: irreversible actions require an exact-payload confirmation gate; abstention routes to a human
hardRules.anchor: EU AI Act Art 14 · SR 11-7 discipline

components.name: Color
components.summary: A near-neutral canvas with one working accent. Consumer color earns attention it doesn't demand: semantic colors mean the same thing on every screen, and no state is ever encoded by hue alone.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.3 contrast (minimum) and 1.4.1 use of color; HIG Color (semantic, adaptive colors); Material 3 color roles.

components.name: Typography
components.summary: Two voices: a tight display face for moments, the native system stack for everything else. Consumer type is generous — bigger minimums, looser leading, tighter tracking as size grows.
components.anchor: HIG Typography (Dynamic Type); Material 3 type scale; WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.4 resize text, 1.4.10 reflow, 1.4.12 text spacing.

components.name: Spacing & Layout
components.summary: A 4px base grid with an 8-step scale. White space is the cheapest premium material there is — this system spends it deliberately.
components.anchor: HIG Layout (44pt targets, safe areas); Material 3 4dp grid; WCAG 2.2 · 2.5.8 target size (minimum).

components.name: Materials & Elevation
components.summary: Three levels of shadow and one glass. Elevation answers exactly one question — what is above what — so it is spent like money.
components.anchor: HIG Materials (vibrancy, translucency); Material 3 elevation; WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.3 contrast over variable backgrounds.

components.name: Motion
components.summary: One spring, three durations. Motion in this system is spatial reasoning — it tells you where things came from and where they went. Anything that only decorates gets cut.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.3.3 animation from interactions, 2.3.1 flash thresholds; HIG Motion; Material 3 motion (emphasized easing).

components.name: Iconography
components.summary: Icons are labels that got shorter, not decoration that got meaning. One family, one optical grid, and a text label whenever the action is destructive or unfamiliar.
components.anchor: HIG SF Symbols conventions (weight-matched, filled-selected); Material Symbols; WCAG 2.2 · 1.1.1 non-text content.

components.name: Haptics & Sound
components.summary: The invisible foundation. A web page can't fire a Taptic Engine, so this entry is the policy layer: when native surfaces of the same product should speak through touch and sound, and when they must stay silent.
components.anchor: HIG Playing haptics ("use haptics consistently, don't overuse"); Material guidance on haptic feedback; WCAG 2.2 · 1.1 perceivable redundancy principle.

components.name: Button
components.summary: The pill is the promise: one obvious next step per view. Everything else steps down in weight until hierarchy does the persuading, not color.
components.anchor: HIG Buttons (prominence hierarchy, 44pt targets); Material 3 button hierarchy; WCAG 2.2 · 2.5.8 target size, 2.4.7 focus visible.

components.name: Text Input
components.summary: Labels stay visible, errors say what to do next, and the keyboard that appears is the one the field deserves. Most abandoned checkouts die in a form.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 3.3.1 error identification, 3.3.2 labels, 3.3.7 redundant entry, 1.3.5 identify input purpose (autocomplete); HIG Text fields.

components.name: Search Field
components.summary: The front door of every catalog, feed, and library. Rounded, iconed, instant — and it never punishes an empty result with a dead end.
components.anchor: HIG Search fields; Material 3 search; WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3 status messages (result counts).

components.name: Select
components.summary: The native picker wearing the system's clothes. On phones the OS wheel and sheet pickers beat anything a div can fake — so this select stays a <select>.
components.anchor: HIG Pickers; Material 3 menus; WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.2 name-role-value (free with native semantics).

components.name: Slider
components.summary: For values where the feel matters more than the digits — volume, brightness, price range. The current value is always readable, never guessed from thumb position.
components.anchor: HIG Sliders; Material 3 sliders; WCAG 2.2 · 2.5.7 dragging movements (keyboard alternative required), 2.5.8 target size.

components.name: Toggle Switch
components.summary: The switch means now — flip it and the thing is on. If anything else must happen first (a save button, a payment), it isn't a switch.
components.anchor: HIG Toggles; Material 3 switch; WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.1 use of color, 4.1.2 name-role-value; GDPR Art 7 — data toggles default off.

components.name: Checkbox & Radio
components.summary: The oldest controls on the web, kept native and kept honest: checkboxes for any-of, radios for one-of, and the whole row is the target.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.3.1 info & relationships (fieldset), 2.5.8 target size; GDPR Art 7(2) — unbundled, unticked consent; ePrivacy consent conventions.

components.name: Segmented Control
components.summary: All the options, all the time. The sliding thumb makes switching feel free — which is exactly when users explore.
components.anchor: HIG Segmented controls; Material 3 segmented buttons; WAI-ARIA radio-group pattern.

components.name: Quantity Stepper
components.summary: Plus, minus, and a number that never surprises you. The humble stepper moves more units of physical goods than any carousel ever will.
components.anchor: HIG Steppers; WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3 status messages, 2.5.8 target size.

components.name: Chip & Tag
components.summary: Small, tappable, and plural. Chips are how consumer products let people say "these, not those" without a form.
components.anchor: Material 3 chips (filter/input/assist); HIG Tokens & tags conventions; WCAG 2.2 · 2.5.8.

components.name: Badge & Count
components.summary: Tiny, loud, and easy to abuse. A badge is a claim on attention — this system rations them like the currency they are.
components.anchor: HIG notification badge conventions; Material 3 badges; WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.1 use of color.

components.name: Avatar & Presence
components.summary: The pixel-sized proof there's a person here. Initials fall back gracefully, groups stack, and the green dot never lies.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.1.1 non-text content, 1.4.1 use of color; GDPR — presence is personal data, off by default where jurisdictions require.

components.name: Card
components.summary: One idea per card, one card per idea. The hover lift is the system's handshake — content rises to meet you, gently.
components.anchor: Material 3 cards; HIG content organisation; WCAG 2.2 · 2.4.4 link purpose in context.

components.name: List & Cell
components.summary: The inset grouped list is the load-bearing wall of every consumer app: settings, inboxes, results, orders. Icon, two lines, trailing detail — a grammar everyone already reads.
components.anchor: HIG Lists and tables (inset grouped); Material 3 lists; WCAG 2.2 · 2.5.8, 1.3.1.

components.name: Tabs
components.summary: Peer views of the same subject, underlined so the floor tells you where you stand. Tabs change the view; the tab bar (see Navigation) changes the world.
components.anchor: WAI-ARIA tabs pattern; Material 3 tabs; HIG segmented alternatives guidance.

components.name: Toast & Snackbar
components.summary: Confirmation that doesn't ask for anything back. Glass pill, four seconds, gone — and when it carries an Undo, it is quietly the most humane component in the system.
components.anchor: Material 3 snackbar; WCAG 2.2 · 2.2.1 timing adjustable, 4.1.3 status messages.

components.name: Modal Dialog
components.summary: The interface's interruption budget, spent one dialog at a time. If the user didn't cause it and can't lose anything, it doesn't get to be modal.
components.anchor: WAI-ARIA dialog pattern; HIG Alerts (outcome-named buttons); WCAG 2.2 · 2.4.3 focus order, 2.1.2 no keyboard trap.

components.name: Bottom Sheet
components.summary: The mobile-native answer to "show me options without leaving." It rises from where thumbs live, and the grabber is a promise: you can always push it back down.
components.anchor: HIG Sheets (detents, grabber); Material 3 bottom sheets; WCAG 2.2 · 2.1.2, 2.5.7 (swipe has button alternative).

components.name: Popover & Tooltip
components.summary: Small truths anchored to the thing they describe. Tooltips name, popovers act — neither ever holds information that exists nowhere else.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.13 content on hover or focus; WAI-ARIA menu & tooltip patterns; HIG Popovers.

components.name: Progress & Loading
components.summary: Honesty about time. Determinate when the end is known, a spinner only when it's short, and a skeleton when there's a shape worth promising.
components.anchor: HIG Progress indicators; Material 3 progress; WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3 status messages.

components.name: Skeleton
components.summary: A promise of shape. The screen commits to its layout before the data arrives, so loading feels like focus resolving rather than construction work.
components.anchor: Material loading guidance; WCAG 2.2 · 2.3.3 animation from interactions; Core Web Vitals CLS discipline.

components.name: Pagination & Dots
components.summary: Numbered pages for destinations you'll cite and return to; dots for carousels you'll drift through. Both tell you where you are — that's the entire job.
components.anchor: HIG Page controls; WCAG 2.2 · 2.4.8 location, 4.1.2 name-role-value.

components.name: Accordion
components.summary: Progressive disclosure on native semantics. Built on <details>, so it works with JavaScript disabled, and searchable-in-page in modern browsers.
components.anchor: WAI-ARIA disclosure pattern (native <details>); WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.2; HIG disclosure controls.

components.name: Empty State
components.summary: The first screen most new users actually see. An empty state is onboarding wearing casual clothes — it names the value and hands over the first move.
components.anchor: Material empty state guidance; NN/g empty-state conventions; WCAG 2.2 · 2.4.6 headings and labels.

components.name: Banner & Inline Alert
components.summary: Persistent context that waits. Where a toast taps you on the shoulder and leaves, a banner sits down until the situation changes.
components.anchor: Material 3 banners; WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3 status messages, 1.4.1 use of color.

components.name: Date & Time Picker
components.summary: The control people fight with most, because it is the one place a product insists on its own format instead of accepting yours. Take typing. Take pasting. Take “next Friday” if you can.
components.anchor: WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices · Date Picker Dialog; WCAG 2.2 · 2.1.1 keyboard, 3.3.2 labels or instructions; HIG Pickers; Material 3 Date pickers.

components.name: File & Photo Upload
components.summary: Uploading is the moment a user hands you something they cannot easily replace. Show the file before you take it, show the progress while you take it, and let them take it back.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3 status messages, 3.3.1 error identification; HIG Photos & camera access; App Store Review 5.1.1 (purpose strings); GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) data minimisation — location EXIF is personal data.

components.name: Multi-Step Flow
components.summary: Long forms survive by lying about their length — honestly. Chunk by topic, show where you are, and make Back free: nothing typed is ever lost to navigation.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 3.3.7 redundant entry, 2.4.3 focus order; checkout-flow conventions (Baymard).

components.name: Stats & Sparkline Card
components.summary: Consumer analytics — screen time, spending, steps — is one number, one direction, one tiny chart. The card answers "how am I doing" before the eye finishes landing on it.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.1, 1.1.1; chart-honesty conventions (labelled ranges, honest baselines).

components.name: Coach Marks & Tips
components.summary: Teaching without a classroom: one anchored tip, at the moment of relevance, dismissed forever with one tap. The feature tour that respects that nobody wants a tour.
components.anchor: HIG onboarding (teach in context); Material feature-discovery guidance; WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.13.

components.name: Address Form
components.summary: The most abandoned form in commerce, and the most international. One search field does most of the work; the rest adapts to the country instead of arguing with it.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.3.5 identify input purpose, 3.3.7; postal-format conventions (UPU); Baymard address research.

components.name: Appearance Switcher
components.summary: Light, dark, or follow the system — with the system as the default, because the user already told their OS what they want and asking twice is a bug.
components.anchor: HIG dark mode; Material color schemes; WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.3 (both themes), prefers-color-scheme.

components.name: Language & Region
components.summary: Every language names itself in itself — 日本語, not "Japanese" — because the person who needs the switch is precisely the one who can't read your current language.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 3.1.2 language of parts; BCP 47; HIG internationalization; W3C i18n best practices.

components.name: Date & Time Picker
components.summary: The control people fight with most, because it is the one place a product insists on its own format instead of accepting yours. Take typing. Take pasting. Take “next Friday” if you can.
components.anchor: WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices · Date Picker Dialog; WCAG 2.2 · 2.1.1 keyboard, 3.3.2 labels or instructions; HIG Pickers; Material 3 Date pickers.

components.name: Upload & Camera
components.summary: Uploading is the moment a user hands you something they cannot easily replace. Show the file before you take it, show the progress while you take it, and let them take it back.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3 status messages, 3.3.1 error identification; HIG Photos & camera access; App Store Review 5.1.1 (purpose strings); GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) data minimisation — location EXIF is personal data.

components.name: Multi-Step Form
components.summary: Splitting a long form into steps does not make it shorter. It makes it survivable — but only if the user can see how far it goes, go back without loss, and leave without starting over.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.4.3 focus order, 3.3.4 error prevention, 3.3.7 redundant entry (don't ask twice for what you already have); Material 3 Steppers; NN/g progressive disclosure.

components.name: Coach Mark
components.summary: A tooltip you didn't ask for. It is the most abused component in consumer software, so it gets the strictest rule in this system: one, at the moment it is useful, dismissible forever.
components.anchor: HIG Onboarding (“teach in context”); WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.13 content on hover or focus, 2.1.2 no keyboard trap; Material 3 Tooltips (rich).

components.name: Navigation Bar
components.summary: Glass over content: the bar defers to the page scrolling beneath it, and the active pill answers "where am I" without a map.
components.anchor: HIG Navigation bars; WCAG 2.2 · 2.4.1 bypass blocks, 2.4.8 location.

components.name: Tab Bar
components.summary: Five doors at the bottom of the world. The tab bar is the most valuable real estate in a consumer app — every slot must earn daily use.
components.anchor: HIG Tab bars; Material 3 navigation bar (label conventions); WCAG 2.2 · 2.4.8.

components.name: Drawer & Side Menu
components.summary: The overflow home for secondary destinations — account, orders, help, legal. A drawer is where things go so the tab bar doesn't have to lie about their importance.
components.anchor: Material 3 navigation drawer; WCAG 2.2 · 2.1.2 no keyboard trap, 4.1.2.

components.name: Breadcrumb
components.summary: The paper trail through a deep catalog. Mostly a desktop commerce citizen — on phones the back button carries this weight.
components.anchor: WAI-ARIA breadcrumb pattern; schema.org BreadcrumbList (SEO); WCAG 2.2 · 2.4.8.

components.name: Floating Action Button
components.summary: One verb, promoted above the page. The FAB works when the screen has an obvious main thing to do — compose, add, capture — and fails everywhere else.
components.anchor: Material 3 FAB; WCAG 2.2 · 2.5.8 target size, 2.4.7 focus visible.

components.name: Large Title Header
components.summary: The title starts as a headline and condenses into chrome as you scroll — orientation you feel rather than read. Scroll the demo.
components.anchor: HIG Navigation bars (large titles); WCAG 2.2 · 1.3.1 heading structure.

components.name: Welcome Flow
components.summary: Three screens, one promise each, and a skip that actually works. The best onboarding is mostly the product, sooner.
components.anchor: HIG Onboarding ("get to the app quickly"); Material onboarding guidance; WCAG 2.2 · 2.5.7 dragging movements.

components.name: Sign-in & SSO
components.summary: The fewest keystrokes between a person and their account. Platform sign-in first, email as the dignified fallback, passwords as the last resort they've become.
components.anchor: App Store Review Guideline 4.8 (offering an equivalent privacy-respecting login option); provider brand guidelines; WCAG 2.2 · 3.3.8 accessible authentication.

components.name: One-Time Code
components.summary: Six boxes and thirty anxious seconds. Everything about this component exists to make the code arrive, paste, and verify itself.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 3.3.8 accessible authentication (minimum); HIG security code AutoFill conventions.

components.name: Passkey Prompt
components.summary: The end of passwords, sold in one card. The design job is trust: say what a passkey is in one sentence, and make "not now" a real choice.
components.anchor: FIDO2 / WebAuthn UX conventions; HIG passkeys guidance; WCAG 2.2 · 3.3.8 (passkeys are the compliant path).

components.name: Profile Setup
components.summary: Ask little, explain why, skip everything. Every optional field completed here is a gift the user gave you — design like you know it.
components.anchor: GDPR Art 5(1)(c) data minimisation; App Store Guideline 5.1.1 (don't require unneeded personal data); WCAG 2.2 · 3.3.2.

components.name: Permission Primer
components.summary: You get one shot at the OS permission dialog. The primer spends its own screen to make sure you take that shot at the moment the user already wants to say yes.
components.anchor: HIG "request permission at the moment of need"; Play policy on prominent disclosure; GDPR Art 6 purpose limitation.

components.name: Consent Manager
components.summary: The component regulators read first. Reject is as easy as accept, defaults are off, and the toggles do what they say — consent here is a designed artifact, not a legal speed bump.
components.anchor: GDPR Art 7 & Recital 32 (freely given, specific, unambiguous); ePrivacy; CCPA/CPRA opt-out rights; EU DSA Art 25 (no deceptive interface design).

components.name: Paywall & Plans
components.summary: The most scrutinised screen in any subscription app — by users, by app review, by the FTC. This one converts by being legible: real prices, real terms, restore always visible.
components.anchor: App Store Review Guideline 3.1.2 (subscription clarity) & Schedule 2 rules; Play subscriptions policy; FTC Negative Option Rule (clear disclosure before billing).

components.name: Product Card
components.summary: The unit of browsing. Image leads, price never hides, and the save affordance floats where thumbs already are.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.4.4 link purpose; FTC truth-in-advertising (scarcity claims must be true); schema.org Product markup.

components.name: Price Display
components.summary: Tabular, truthful, and complete. A price is a fact with typography — strikethroughs need a real former price, and the number you show is the number they pay.
components.anchor: FTC Guides Against Deceptive Pricing (16 CFR 233); EU Price Indication Directive (prior-price rules); WCAG 2.2 · 1.3.1.

components.name: Cart Line Item
components.summary: Where second thoughts happen. Every line item makes changing your mind cheap — adjust, save for later, remove — because a trapped cart is an abandoned cart.
components.anchor: FTC Section 5 unfairness (pre-checked add-ons); WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3; Baymard cart usability conventions.

components.name: Checkout Summary
components.summary: No math surprises. Every fee has a name, the total is the largest number on screen, and it matches the charge to the cent.
components.anchor: FTC junk-fee rulemaking (all-in pricing); EU Consumer Rights Directive Art 6 (total cost pre-order); WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3.

components.name: Payment Method
components.summary: Radio rows for money. Wallets first (they convert best and typo least), saved cards next, new card last — and the selected row is unmistakable.
components.anchor: PCI-DSS display rules (last four only); card-network brand guidelines; WCAG 2.2 · 3.3.8 (no card-number memory tests).

components.name: Promo Code
components.summary: A tiny form with outsized feelings. Success celebrates with the exact amount saved; failure explains without blaming.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 3.3.1, 3.3.3 error suggestion, 4.1.3; FTC advertised-discount truthfulness.

components.name: Ratings & Reviews
components.summary: Social proof with a chain of custody. Stars summarise, distributions tell the truth, and "verified purchase" means the system checked.
components.anchor: FTC Rule on Consumer Reviews and Testimonials (16 CFR 465); Consumer Review Fairness Act; WCAG 2.2 · 1.3.1.

components.name: Save & Wishlist
components.summary: The lowest-commitment yes in commerce. A save is a bookmark on desire — instant, reversible, synced, and never guilt-tripped.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.2 name-role-value; GDPR-conscious local-first storage; HIG feedback conventions.

components.name: Order Tracking
components.summary: The screen people open eleven times for one package. Its whole job is a truthful answer to "where is it and when" — everything else is decoration.
components.anchor: FTC Mail Order Rule (shipment timing representations); WCAG 2.2 · 1.3.1, 1.4.1.

components.name: Subscription Management
components.summary: The screen that decides whether a customer trusts you, because it is where they find out what you have been charging them and whether you made it hard to stop.
components.anchor: FTC negative-option / click-to-cancel rulemaking (cancel as easy as sign-up; confirm dates with counsel); EU Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83 (pre-contract information); App Store Review 3.1.2; Google Play Subscriptions policy.

components.name: Feed Post
components.summary: The atom of the social web: who, what, and three verbs. The layout is a contract with the reader — authorship always above content, actions always below it.
components.anchor: FTC Endorsement Guides (ad disclosure); WCAG 2.2 · 1.1.1, 4.1.2; EU DSA transparency for recommender systems.

components.name: Comment Thread
components.summary: Conversation with indentation as grammar. One level of nesting reads as reply; two reads as argument; three reads as nothing at all — so this system stops at one.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.3.1; EU DSA Art 16 (notice mechanisms adjacent to content); community-safety conventions.

components.name: Reaction Bar
components.summary: Six feelings on a glass shelf. The long-press reveal is one of the small delights consumer software is allowed — spent here because reacting is frequent, safe, and reversible.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.5.7 dragging/press alternatives; WAI-ARIA toolbar pattern; HIG feedback conventions.

components.name: Share Sheet
components.summary: Distribution's front door. People first, then platforms, then plumbing (copy link) — ordered by what the user does, not what growth wants.
components.anchor: HIG activity views (share sheets); Web Share API conventions; WCAG 2.2 · 2.1.1.

components.name: Chat Bubbles
components.summary: Two voices, two sides, zero ambiguity. Yours right and tinted, theirs left and neutral — a convention so strong that breaking it reads as a bug.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3, 1.4.3; EU AI Act transparency (bot disclosure); messaging privacy norms (GDPR).

components.name: Notification Item
components.summary: A sentence with a face. Actor, verb, object, time — and unread state you can see from across the room. The list is an inbox, so it behaves like one.
components.anchor: HIG Notifications ("valuable, not promotional"); Play FCM policy; WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.1.

components.name: Follow Button
components.summary: The smallest social contract. Following is loud, followed is quiet — the state change is the entire design, so it must be unmistakable and reversible in one tap.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.2, 1.4.1; platform anti-spam norms (no auto-follow).

components.name: Story Ring
components.summary: A gradient halo that means "new, and it expires." The seen state — gray, quiet — is just as much the design as the rainbow.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.1, 2.1.1; ephemeral-content honesty conventions.

components.name: Profile Header
components.summary: A person's front door: identity above the fold, numbers that mean something, one primary action. Everything else on the profile is furniture — this is the handshake.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.3.1 headings, 2.4.4 link purpose; EU DSA Art 30 (trader identity where accounts sell); verified-badge conventions (see Trust & Safety).

components.name: Message Inbox
components.summary: The conversation list is triage, not archaeology: who, the last line, how long ago, and whether it needs you — readable in a glance per row. Strangers wait in Requests, not in your face.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.5.7 dragging movements, 1.4.1; ePrivacy (unsolicited messaging consent); platform anti-spam norms.

components.name: Poll & Voting
components.summary: The lightest form of speech. One tap to vote, results the moment you have — and never the moment before, because seeing the crowd first changes the answer.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.1, 4.1.3; research-method honesty (no result-peeking bias); EU DSA Art 25.

components.name: Mentions & Hashtags
components.summary: The wiring of the social graph: @ points at a person, # points at a room. Both are entities the moment they're typed — colored, linked, and accountable.
components.anchor: WAI-ARIA combobox pattern; WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.1; EU DSA (notice mechanisms extend to tags of people).

components.name: Live Stream Chat
components.summary: Thousands of voices in a phone-width column. The design job is legibility under flood: pinned context stays put, moderation is one tap, and the flow never steals your scroll position.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3 (throttled announcements), 2.2.2; EU DSA Art 16 (report adjacency); App Store 1.2 (UGC moderation).

components.name: Link Preview Card
components.summary: The unfurled URL: image, title, domain. Its one non-negotiable job is telling the truth about where a tap will take you — the domain is the security surface, not a caption.
components.anchor: Open Graph conventions; FTC deception standard (misleading destinations); WCAG 2.2 · 2.4.4.

components.name: Video Player Controls
components.summary: Controls that get out of the way and come back when called. Everything essential within one thumb arc: play, scrub, captions, volume.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.2.2 captions, 2.2.2 pause/stop/hide; HIG playback; Media Session API conventions.

components.name: Mini Player
components.summary: Playback that follows you around the app without blocking it. A glass bar above the tab bar: art, title, play, next — and a tap expands to the full stage.
components.anchor: HIG now-playing conventions; WCAG 2.2 · 2.5.7, 4.1.2.

components.name: Gallery & Lightbox
components.summary: A grid that promises and a lightbox that delivers. The grid is uniform and dense; the lightbox is the one place chrome fully yields to the image.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.5.7, 1.1.1; HIG image viewing conventions.

components.name: Carousel
components.summary: Scroll-snap, native momentum, and a peek of the next slide doing the affordance work. The browser already knows how to swipe — this component just stops fighting it.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.2.2 pause/stop/hide; CSS scroll-snap conventions; NN/g carousel research.

components.name: Live Badge
components.summary: Two words that must never lie: LIVE means now, and the pulse means the signal is real. The moment the stream ends, the badge dies with it.
components.anchor: FTC deception standard (liveness claims); WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.1, 2.3.3.

components.name: Captions
components.summary: Most video is watched silent; captions are the soundtrack most people actually use. High contrast, two lines, and never covering the faces they transcribe.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.2.2 captions (prerecorded), 1.2.4 (live); FCC caption quality rules; CVAA.

components.name: Onboarding Checklist
components.summary: Progress you can feel. The checklist turns "set up your account" from a lecture into a game the user is already winning — because the first item arrives pre-checked.
components.anchor: Endowed progress research (Nunes & Drèze); WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3; EU DSA Art 25 (no manipulative pressure).

components.name: Streak & Achievement
components.summary: Celebration without hostage-taking. A streak marks showing up; this one is designed so missing a day stings less than the habit is worth.
components.anchor: EU DSA Art 25; FTC dark-pattern report (guilt-driven engagement); WCAG 2.2 · 2.3.3.

components.name: Referral Card
components.summary: Both sides of the deal on one card. Referrals work when the invitation is a gift, not an extraction — so the friend's reward leads.
components.anchor: FTC endorsement rules (incentivised referrals disclose); CAN-SPAM / TCPA (user-initiated sends); WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.5.

components.name: Push Pre-Prompt
components.summary: Permission with a menu. Instead of "allow notifications?", the primer asks which — orders only, or the social noise too — and the OS prompt fires only after a real yes.
components.anchor: HIG asking permission; Android notification channels; Play FCM policy; ePrivacy (marketing push is consent-based).

components.name: In-App Review Prompt
components.summary: Ask happy people, once, at the right moment — and never intercept the unhappy into a private complaint box while herding fans to the store. That fork is now a violation, not a growth hack.
components.anchor: FTC 16 CFR 465.4 (review suppression); App Store Guideline 1.1.7 & SKStoreReviewController limits; Play in-app review API rules.

components.name: Survey & NPS
components.summary: One question, honestly asked, instantly dismissible. Survey fatigue is a design failure — this component is rationed like the interruption it is.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.3.1, 4.1.3; research-ethics conventions (voluntary, no dark nudges).

components.name: What's New
components.summary: Release notes people might actually read: three items, verbs first, each row deep-linking to the feature it announces. Shown once, then it's a page, not a prompt.
components.anchor: HIG onboarding & release-note conventions; WCAG 2.2 · 2.4.4.

components.name: Report & Block
components.summary: The exits from a bad interaction, always two taps away. Report feeds the system; block protects the person — the component never confuses whose problem each solves.
components.anchor: EU DSA Art 16 (notice and action) & Art 20 (appeals); App Store Guideline 1.2 (UGC apps must have report/block); Play UGC policy.

components.name: Content Warning
components.summary: A blur that respects both the viewer and the content. It names the category, offers the choice, and remembers the preference — informed consent at feed speed.
components.anchor: EU DSA systemic-risk mitigation; App Store 1.2 / Play sensitive-content rules; WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.3.

components.name: Age Gate
components.summary: A door, not a decoration. Where children's privacy law applies, the gate is designed to be neutral — it doesn't wink, hint, or make the underage path retryable until it passes.
components.anchor: COPPA · 16 CFR Part 312 (neutral age screening, FTC guidance); GDPR Art 8; UK Age Appropriate Design Code.

components.name: Privacy Dashboard
components.summary: Every promise the consent screen made, auditable in one place. What's collected, why, and the switch to stop it — the settings page as a trust document.
components.anchor: GDPR Arts 13–15 (transparency & access); CCPA right to know; Apple privacy nutrition labels (App Store 5.1).

components.name: Data Rights
components.summary: Download everything, delete everything — as self-service buttons, not support tickets. The delete flow states its consequences once, plainly, then does what it says.
components.anchor: GDPR Art 17 (erasure) & 20 (portability); CCPA deletion right; App Store 5.1.1(v) — account deletion in-app if creation is in-app.

components.name: Verified Badge
components.summary: A checkmark is a claim the platform makes with its own reputation. This one means identity was checked — never that content is true, and never that a fee was paid unless the label says so.
components.anchor: EU DSA Art 25 & trader traceability (Art 30); FTC deception standard; WCAG 2.2 · 1.1.1.

components.name: Security Checkup
components.summary: An annual physical for the account, readable in ten seconds. Green means done, amber means one tap to fix — and the score never shames, it invites.
components.anchor: NIST 800-63 authenticator guidance; WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.1; platform account-security conventions.

components.name: Account Deletion
components.summary: A door that only opens inwards is not a door. If a user can create an account in the app, they must be able to end it in the app — and know exactly what that ends.
components.anchor: App Store Review 5.1.1(v) — in-app account deletion is required; Google Play Data deletion policy (in-app and web route); GDPR Art. 17 right to erasure and Art. 20 portability; CCPA/CPRA deletion rights.

components.name: AI Composer
components.summary: The blank box is the hardest interface in consumer software: infinite capability, zero affordance. The composer's job is not to look clever — it is to tell you what this thing can do and where its edges are, before you waste a turn finding out.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 3.3.2 labels or instructions, 2.1.1 keyboard; EU AI Act Art. 50 transparency (the user must know they are interacting with an AI system); HIG Machine Learning — set expectations, show the limits.

components.name: Streaming Response
components.summary: Streaming solves latency and creates an accessibility problem in the same instant: text that changes sixty times a second is unusable to a screen reader. The fix is to stream to the eye and announce to the ear once.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3 status messages, 2.2.2 pause, stop, hide (moving content); ARIA live-region practice; prefers-reduced-motion for the caret.

components.name: Sources & Citations
components.summary: A citation is not decoration. It is the difference between an answer you can check and an answer you must simply believe — and a fabricated citation is worse than none, because it buys trust it hasn't earned.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.4.4 link purpose, 1.4.1 use of colour; FTC guidance on substantiation and deceptive claims; EU AI Act Art. 50 transparency; NIST AI RMF (Measure — traceability of outputs).

components.name: Confidence & Abstention
components.summary: The most valuable thing an AI product can say is “I don't know — here is someone who does.” Abstention is a feature. A confidently wrong answer costs more than no answer, and it costs the user, not you.
components.anchor: NIST AI RMF (Manage — risk-informed escalation); EU AI Act Art. 14 human oversight (high-risk uses); WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.1 use of colour; FTC Section 5 — unsubstantiated capability claims.

components.name: AI Disclosure
components.summary: If it was generated, say so — on the artefact, at the moment of viewing, in a form that survives a screenshot's worth of doubt. This is now law in some markets and it will be law in more.
components.anchor: EU AI Act Art. 50 (transparency; machine-readable marking of synthetic content — confirm dates and scope with counsel); C2PA Content Credentials 2.x; FTC guidance on AI claims and endorsements; platform synthetic-media policies.

components.name: Agent Action Confirmation
components.summary: An agent that can act on your behalf is a system that can be wrong on your behalf. The interface question is not “how do we make this smooth” — it is which actions a human must sign, and how we make that signature meaningful rather than reflexive.
components.anchor: EU AI Act Art. 14 human oversight; NIST AI RMF (Govern — accountability for automated actions); PSD2 SCA for payment initiation; WCAG 2.2 · 3.3.4 error prevention (legal, financial, data).

components.name: Agent Activity Trace
components.summary: When something acts for you while you are not looking, the receipt is the product. A trace is how a user audits a decision they didn't watch — and how they find the moment it went wrong.
components.anchor: EU AI Act Art. 12 record-keeping / logging; NIST AI RMF (Measure — traceability); GDPR Art. 22 (a route to contest an automated decision needs a record of it); SR 11-7 effective challenge, in the regulated sibling of this system.

components.name: Prompt Starters
components.summary: Starters are not decoration on an empty state — they are the only honest documentation an AI surface has. Each one is a promise: this is a thing I can actually do.
components.anchor: HIG Machine Learning — “set expectations, offer examples”; WCAG 2.2 · 2.4.6 headings and labels, 2.5.8 target size; NN/g empty-state guidance.

components.name: Feedback & Correction
components.summary: A thumbs-down that goes into a dashboard nobody reads is a complaint box in an empty building. Feedback earns its place only if the user can see what it changed — at minimum, for them.
components.anchor: GDPR Art. 16 right to rectification (if the output is personal data, correction is a right, not a courtesy); DSA Art. 16 notice-and-action for illegal content; NIST AI RMF (Manage — incident feedback loops); WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.2 name, role, value.

components.name: Memory & Context
components.summary: An assistant that remembers is useful. An assistant that remembers invisibly is surveillance with a friendly voice. The rule is simple: if it remembered it, you can read it, and you can delete it.
components.anchor: GDPR Art. 5 (purpose limitation, minimisation), Art. 9 (special categories), Art. 17 erasure; CCPA/CPRA right to delete; App Store Privacy Nutrition Labels; COPPA (no behavioural profiling of children).

components.name: Training & Personalisation
components.summary: Two different questions get collapsed into one toggle by most products, and it is not an accident: “use my data to personalise my experience” and “use my data to train your model” are not the same deal.
components.anchor: GDPR Art. 7 (freely given, unbundled, as easy to withdraw), Art. 21 objection, Art. 22 automated decisions; EU AI Act transparency duties; App Tracking Transparency; COPPA (verifiable parental consent).

components.name: AI Summary in Search
components.summary: Summarising other people's work at the top of a results page is a redistribution of attention. Do it in a way that still sends the reader — and the credit — onward.
components.anchor: EU AI Act Art. 50 transparency; FTC guidance on deceptive presentation; WCAG 2.2 · 2.4.1 bypass blocks, 1.3.1 info and relationships; copyright and DSM Art. 15 press-publisher rights — substance, not just attribution.

components.name: Refusal & Escalation
components.summary: Every AI product eventually meets the request it should not answer. The design question is what happens in that second — because a refusal with no exit is just a door closing on someone who came to you for help.
components.anchor: EU AI Act Art. 14 human oversight; DSA Art. 20 internal complaint-handling; App Store Review 1.1/5.1 (safety and sensitive content); NIST AI RMF (Manage — escalation and incident response).

components.name: Voice Agent
components.summary: Voice removes the screen, and with it every affordance you were relying on. What is left has to carry the whole contract: that it is listening, that it is a machine, and that you can cut it off.
components.anchor: EU AI Act Art. 50 (a person must be told they are talking to an AI); two-party-consent recording laws (e.g. CA Penal Code §632 — confirm per jurisdiction with counsel); WCAG 2.2 · 1.2.4 captions (live), 2.5.4 motion actuation; HIG Siri & voice.

components.name: Tool & Data Grants
components.summary: The permission surface of the MCP era. An agent's power comes from its tools — so every tool and every data source is its own grant: scoped, separately revocable, and visible in one place. "Allow everything" is not a setting, it's a surrender.
components.anchor: GDPR Art 5(1)(c) & 6 (purpose limitation — a grant is a purpose); EU AI Act Art 14 human oversight; least-privilege conventions from OAuth scope design.

components.name: Background Agent Tasks
components.summary: Agents work in minutes, not milliseconds — so the queue is a first-class surface. Four honest states: queued, working, needs you, done. "Needs you" is the interesting one — it means the agent hit a gate and stopped, which is the system working, not failing.
components.anchor: EU AI Act Art 14 (interruptibility as effective oversight); WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3 status messages; HIG background task conventions.

components.name: Mode & Model Picker
components.summary: Fast or thorough is a real decision users can make — if the trade-off is stated in outcomes, not model names. Nobody should need to know what a parameter count is to choose how carefully their question gets answered.
components.anchor: EU AI Act Art 50 transparency; FTC clarity on charges (paid modes state their price at the decision point); WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.2.

components.name: Ghost Text & Suggested Edits
components.summary: The most intimate AI surface: inside the user's own sentence. The contract is absolute — suggested text is unmistakably not-yet-yours, accepting it is always an explicit act, and your words are never overwritten.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.1 use of color, 2.1.1 keyboard; HIG Machine Learning — corrections (user stays the author).

components.name: Human ↔ Agent Handoff
components.summary: When an agent can drive a session — filling a form, working a screen — exactly one question must never be ambiguous: who is driving right now. The handoff banner answers it at all times, and the wheel is always within reach.
components.anchor: EU AI Act Art 14 (oversight must be effective, not nominal — interruptibility is the test); WCAG 2.2 · 2.1.1; EU AI Act Art 50 (the agent's presence is disclosed).

components.name: Usage & Cost Meter
components.summary: AI features have a meter running, and hiding it is a pricing dark pattern with extra steps. The meter shows what's spent, what's left, and — critically — what happens at the cap, before the cap.
components.anchor: FTC all-in pricing discipline (the cost is disclosed where it's incurred); App Store 3.1 (in-app purchase clarity); WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3, 1.4.1.

components.name: Generated Artifact Card
components.summary: When AI output is a thing — an image, a document, an itinerary — it stops being a message and becomes an object with duties: versions that don't destroy each other, provenance you can open, and a disclosure that survives export.
components.anchor: EU AI Act Art 50 (synthetic content marking); C2PA 2.x content credentials; GDPR Art 17 (deleting an artifact deletes its versions).

components.name: Capability Disclosure
components.summary: The first screen of any AI feature decides every later disappointment. Three things it can do, three it can't, one line about data — the anti-magic show. Underclaiming here is the cheapest trust you will ever buy.
components.anchor: EU AI Act Art 50 transparency; FTC deception standard (capability claims); HIG Machine Learning — set accurate expectations.

components.name: Status Orb
components.summary: A spinner has one state: “working.” An agent has many — listening, thinking, searching, writing code, done — and telling them apart is the difference between a user who waits and a user who understands why. The orb encodes agent state as motion, not just presence.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.3.3 animation from interactions, 1.4.1 use of colour (state is not colour-only — pair with the status text); prefers-reduced-motion freezes the current frame rather than hiding the element; ARIA role=img with a state-derived accessible name kept in sync via aria-live status text.

components.name: Pull to Refresh
components.summary: The gesture that taught a generation how feeds work. Pull, arm, release — with a visible threshold so the hand always knows whether letting go will act.
components.anchor: HIG refresh content controls; WCAG 2.2 · 2.5.7 dragging movements, 4.1.3.

components.name: Infinite Scroll vs Pages
components.summary: Infinite scroll is a loan against the user's sense of time. This system spends it only where content is truly endless — and always installs a footer the scroll can land on.
components.anchor: EU DSA Art 25 & recital 67 (attention-exploiting design); WCAG 2.2 · 2.4.1; NN/g infinite-scroll research.

components.name: Undo, Not Confirm
components.summary: Confirmation dialogs make everyone pay a tax because someone might err. Undo charges only the error, only when it happens — act immediately, offer the way back.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.2.1 timing adjustable, 3.3.4 error prevention; HIG undo conventions; NN/g forgiveness principle.

components.name: Error Recovery
components.summary: Errors are moments of maximum attention — the one time you're guaranteed a careful reader. Say what happened, what it cost, and what to do, in that order.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 3.3.1, 3.3.3; NN/g error-message guidelines.

components.name: Offline Mode
components.summary: The network is a feature the world sometimes turns off. Offline design keeps reading, queues writing, and tells the truth about both.
components.anchor: HIG & Material offline guidance; WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3; PWA offline-first conventions.

components.name: Cancellation Flow
components.summary: The truest test of a product's ethics: leaving must be as easy as arriving. One path, two screens, zero guilt — the FTC calls it click-to-cancel; this system calls it the default.
components.anchor: FTC Negative Option Rule (click-to-cancel); App Store 3.1.2 / Play subscription cancellation rules; EU Consumer Rights Directive.

components.name: Search & Filter
components.summary: Query, refine, count — the loop behind every marketplace. Filters are chips you can see and remove one at a time; the result count updates with every change so cause never loses its effect.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 4.1.3, 2.5.8; EU DSA Art 27 (ranking transparency); Baymard filtering conventions.

components.name: Split Reveal
components.summary: The headline arrives one character at a time — a stagger so short it reads as texture, not theatre. The workhorse entrance for hero copy.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.3.3 animation from interactions; Core Web Vitals CLS discipline; HIG Motion (purposeful, brief).

components.name: Blur In
components.summary: Words resolve from soft focus to sharp, like the eye settling. The gentlest entrance in the set — calm products earn it.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.3.3; vestibular-safe motion guidance (filter over transform); HIG Motion.

components.name: Typewriter
components.summary: Text that appears to be written, caret and all. Fifty years old and still the most honest way to say "something is composing this."
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.2.2 (nothing blinks indefinitely), 2.3.3; EU AI Act Art 50 adjacency (composition theatre must be truthful).

components.name: Decode
components.summary: Characters churn through noise and settle into the message, left to right. The cyberpunk entrance — loud, memorable, and strictly rationed.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.3.3, 4.1.3 (announce once, final only); Core Web Vitals CLS.

components.name: Count Up
components.summary: Numbers that travel to their value. Movement says "this was measured, watch it arrive" — which is exactly why it may only ever land on the true figure.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.3.3, 4.1.3; FTC substantiation discipline (motion is emphasis — emphasised claims need evidence).

components.name: Word Rotate
components.summary: One slot in the sentence cycles through alternatives — "built for runners / riders / climbers". The rotation makes a list feel like a welcome.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.2.2 pause/stop/hide (self-stopping), 2.3.3; FTC (rotating claims are still claims).

components.name: Gradient Flow
components.summary: A slow aurora inside the letterforms. Color moves so the type doesn't have to — the quietest way to make one line feel alive.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.3 (every stop passes), 2.3.3; HIG color (decorative color never carries meaning).

components.name: Shine Sweep
components.summary: A highlight passes across the word once, like light across brushed metal. The premium accent — and like all premium things, scarce by design.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 1.4.3 (base state passes alone), 2.3.3; EU DSA Art 25 (no shimmer-as-urgency).

components.name: Wave
components.summary: Characters take turns bouncing — playful energy for playful products. The party trick of the set, which is precisely why it self-stops.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.2.2 (self-stopping), 2.3.3; UK Age Appropriate Design Code adjacency (kid surfaces avoid compulsive motion).

components.name: Marquee Ticker
components.summary: The infinite ribbon — logos, headlines, drop announcements. The only permanently moving text this system allows, and it pays for the privilege with a real pause control.
components.anchor: WCAG 2.2 · 2.2.2 pause/stop/hide (the letter of it), 2.3.3; HIG Motion.

tokenNotes.contrast: text tokens hold >= 4.5:1 on their surfaces in both themes (WCAG 2.2 AA)
tokenNotes.motion: --spring is the single house curve; all animation is gated behind prefers-reduced-motion
tokenNotes.usage: components must reference tokens, never raw hex
